To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mouse liver nicotinamid N-methyltransferse (NNMT) has biochemical properties very similar to those reported for human liver NNMT and that NNMT activity varies widely in hepatic cytoplasm from male mice of different strains and in hepatic cytoosol from female mice of different strains.

(1) Mouse liver NNMT is an important cytosolic enzyme that is responsible for the in vivo methylation of nicotinate and nicotinamide; (2) NNMT activity in mouse liver is highly variable among inbred mouse strains and among genders within strains; (3) This enzyme shows large individual variations in humans, as does NNMT activity in human liver; (4) The properties of NNMT in mouse liver are very similar to those in human liver.

the development of a model for the pharmacogenetics of the N-methotransferase enzyme, nicotinamide-N-methyltransferase, in mice.

The main takeaway from our work is that

NNMT activity in mice varies by more than 10-fold among inbred strains, and that the enzyme is a cytoplasmically localized, pH optimum 7.4, S-adenosylethionine-dependent, nicotinamide-specific methyltransferase with properties that are similar to those of the human liver enzyme.
